newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - March 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - March 7.

text.p: Serious Fraud Office director Chas Sturt canned an injury into the BNZ in April 1993 because "our friends in Wellington would not appreciate the office inquiring into the Bank of New Zealand." In particular, Sturt told his chief investigator Geoff Downey, he "did not want to give Winston Peters any further ammunition or cause in regards to his call for an inquiry into the bank." Downey -- a former police colleague of Sturt's in the 1960s -- told the winebox Commission of Inquiry on Thursday that he had "no doubt" the director's "friends in Wellington" referred to "members of the National party, who were then in government." Page 1.

Police and Companies Office officials are investigating Savannah Ostrich Processing Company, after Kiwi investors found themselves the losers in a trans-Tasman argument between two brothers. On this side of the Tasman is John Lagettie, and Australian racing enthusiast and owner and director of Savannah Ostrich Processing Company and other related ostrich investment companies. On the other side of the Tasman, David Lagettie, owner and director of Monaroo Farm in New South Wales, was to have bought the big birds on behalf of the investors. Page 1.
The Aotearoa TV saga took a bizarre twist this week when a NZ First staffer was caught impersonating a journalist at a press conference given by Labour MP Trevor Mallard. Page 3.

Rupert Murdoch's decision to launch into the United States pay-tv market may have put the final nail in the coffin of the INL-Sky deal. A bid by Murdoch and INL to buy a controlling stake in Sky came to an abrupt end last week. INL -- 49.9 percent owned by Murdoch's News Corporation -- won't say what sank the deal, which could also have seen TVNZ boost its stake in Sky to just under 25 percent. However, one informed source said things came unstuck when the opportunity arose for Murdoch to buy into EchoStar, one of America's biggest pay-tv operators. EchoStar involved an investment of about $1 billion and "that diverted his attention", the source said. Page 3

Few chief executives would feel like smiling when announcing a 32 percent drop in interim profit. But Brierley Investments boss Paul Collins was in an upbeat mood -- largely because the financial indicator the company most cares about jumped considerably in the six months. BIL on Thursday posted a $116.14 million profit for the December interim, down from $170.02 million. Page 6.

A new Maori television company is rising from the ashes of ill-starred Aotearoa Television Network. Pounamu Greenstone Television is as yet without a frequency, funding or a transmitter. But 20 former ATN staffers are working without wages hoping to establish a viable commercial entity before the government's policy on setting up a Maori television channel is announced mid-year. While it will be seeking some government funding, if available, trustee and well-known broadcaster Paul Holmes says the company will be commercially-focused. Page 6.

Computer retailer PC Direct this week tried and failed to get a High Court injunction preventing its rival Best Buy from using PC Direct's name in knocking advetisements. Justice Elias declined the injunction. Her grounds centred on concern about effective competition and freedom of speech enshrined in the Bill of Rights. Best Buy were also seeking an injunction to stop PC Direct re-publishing its "Consumer Warning" comparative advertisement. PC Direct agreed to desist. Page 7.

It has been a busy fortnight for NZ Post. In addition to signing up as agents for Ergo Financial Services, the former Post Office recently announced a $150 million debt securities issue and now, this week, it has ignored the wowsers by unveiling its latest stamp issue, New Zealand Vineyards. The series, due for release on 19 March, features six vineyeards, one each from Central Otago, Hawkes Bay, Marlborough, Canterbury, Gisborne and Waiheke Island. Page 24.
